SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park.
All summer, Sheets had been playing through a nasty injury -- a plantar plate tear in his left foot. He wondered if he’d be able to contribute at all. There was certainly no way he could contribute defensively.
But maybe … just maybe … if Sheets could heal just enough … he could deliver a meaningful swing or two in the postseason.
A swing like this one.
Sheets came off the bench to deliver the swing that broke the Cubs in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series on Wednesday night -- a pinch-hit, two-run home run that sent Petco Park into delirium and the Padres on course for Milwaukee.
With their 4-1 victory over the Cubs, San Diego secured a trip to the NL Division Series against the Brewers, beginning on Saturday night. But first, the Padres staged a party in the home clubhouse at Petco Park.
Before the champagne was popped and the cigars were lit, manager Craig Stammen stood at the center of it all.
“We had 13 bricks to lay,” Stammen said. “Two down, 11 more to go.”
The next three almost certainly won’t come quite so easily. For the fourth time in seven seasons, the Padres are headed to the NLDS, where they’ll meet Milwaukee in a playoff series for the first time. The Brewers own the sport’s best record. Jacob Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner, takes the ball first.
“We know who they’re throwing Game 1,” said Xander Bogaerts. “So let’s celebrate today. And then be ready for that fastball.”
Call it sweet revenge for the Padres after their 2025 season came to an end with a Wild Card Series exit at Wrigley Field.
They made quick work of the Cubs, dispatching them in two games that were never all that close. The two teams played 18 innings at Petco Park this week. The Padres led after 17 of them. The Chicago offense, which scored more runs than any other team during the regular season, was held to one across two playoff games.
“We just didn't play well enough,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “And they're playing really well.”
In Game 1, the Padres were a force of nature. The ballpark partied from the very first pitch (a Michael King fastball past Pete Crow-Armstrong) to the very last pitch (Joe Musgrove punctuating his triumphant return to the mound with a game-ending strikeout). They won, 8-0.
“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Manny Machado, a veteran of eight postseasons, said of the home crowd this week. “That was huge.”
Game 2 brought a different kind of postseason energy. A party, to be sure. But one with some tension mixed in. October baseball, on the final day of September.
San Diego jumped in front in the second with Bogaerts’ RBI single and Ethan Salas’ sacrifice fly. (Salas, the youngest player in history to catch a postseason game, also became the youngest player at any position with a postseason sac fly -- since at least 1954 when that stat was fully tracked.)
But the Cubs scratched a run back against Nick Pivetta in the fourth and worked their way into the Padres’ bullpen. Crow-Armstrong and the top of the lineup loomed in the fifth.
There were two outs and a runner aboard, and Counsell had gone with right-hander Daniel Palencia. Sheets strode to the on-deck circle, then, eventually, the batter’s box -- with those three familiar thuds echoing through the Petco Park sound system.
HO-LY SHEETS.
“You just get ready for that moment, so when it happens you don’t feel like it’s sped up on you,” Sheets said. “To see this fanbase the whole entire time, I just wanted to get in front of them, I wanted to play. These guys brought it.”
This was the moment the Padres had been planning for. When Sheets is right, he mashes right-handed pitching. He’s a weapon in the clutch and can be a force off the bench.
“We had talked about that move, probably more than I care to admit in my office, with our pro scouting and advanced scouting,” Stammen said. “We felt like Gavin was a good matchup for some of their right-handed pitching. … That’s why we put him on the bench today, just in case he could pop one like that in a big situation.
“Doesn’t always work out that way. But he made us all look good.”
In the end, Sheets would take all of one swing across two games in the series. He made it count.
Palencia threw a 100.8 mph fastball at the bottom of the zone on the inner half. Sheets turned on it -- the hardest pitch any Padre has ever homered on, regular or postseason.
“That’s Dairy Bonds, baby,” said Jackson Merrill, between puffs of a cigar in a raucous Padres clubhouse. “That’s what he does -- 101, down and in. You just don’t see that. That was sick. That was one of the cooler home runs I’ve ever seen.”
And then get ready for that fastball.

NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame.
The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series (also against the Yankees).
But the Bronx Bombers made the short burst of momentum from Contreras feel insignificant when they erupted for six runs in a game-breaking, series-breaking bottom of the sixth inning that sent deafening roars throughout Yankee Stadium and the Red Sox to a 9-2 loss on Wednesday. Those reverberating sounds were a harsh reminder to the Red Sox that this was likely to be their last game of 2026.
With two flat performances in the final two nights of September, during which they were outscored, 18-2, the Red Sox were denied a chance to play in October. It also extended the streak to five straight seasons of no postseason baseball at Fenway Park.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series, and that ended for us tonight,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So it's frustrating. And there's a lot of things you can say, but in the moment, right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it's going to take some time to get over that.”
It will go down as a roller-coaster spring, summer and brief autumn in Boston. There was the 32-46 hole, which the Sox somehow dug out of with a season-altering 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 7 that included a franchise-tying winning streak of 15 games.
Then there was the final month of the regular season, which included injuries to key players and a stunning lack of offense, two themes that carried into the postseason.
“I'm proud of what we accomplished,” said veteran starter Sonny Gray, who took the loss. “Sour taste in your mouth for the ending. But we were left for dead there for a while, and I will definitely remember that run that we went on and what that felt like, because I've never experienced anything like that in my career -- to dig ourselves out of that hole and to put ourselves in this situation, that was a lot of fun.”
For the Red Sox, the fun ended in New York before it even started.
Quite simply, very little went right for the Sox in this two-game sweep at the hands of their rivals, which lacked the drama of last year’s set that went the distance (also won by the Yankees).
“For our season to end the same way that it did last year against our biggest rival, it sucks” said Red Sox lefty Garrett Crochet.
The bottom of the sixth served as a microcosm of the futility and frustration -- the inning that deep-sixed Tracy and his club.
With Contreras creating some energy in the Boston dugout, Tracy tried to add to it by bringing on Crochet for his first appearance in a game since April 25.
Crochet’s quest to get back in time for postseason play after left shoulder woes was a compelling storyline for the Red Sox, but one that didn’t work in real time.
The lefty seemed to get off to a solid start when he struck out Spencer Jones on a sweeper. But catcher Adley Rutschman’s block wasn’t a clean one, and he appeared to hesitate before throwing to first after retrieving the wild pitch. The initial call of out was overturned on replay. Jones then stole second and moved to third on Rutschman’s throwing error.
From there, things devolved. Crochet didn’t get an out and was charged with four runs, though only one of the three hits he allowed was well-struck.
“Personally, to think that I busted my [butt] the past five months, and for it to end that way, on a personal note, it's tough,” said Crochet. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best I could, and I let them down.”
Gray turned in a strong enough start for the Sox, giving up six hits over 4 2/3 innings and leaving with his team down 1-0.
But the offense never quite came around, and the bullpen had a second straight spotty night. And just like that, the season was over.
“Obviously disappointed,” said shortstop Trevor Story. “A lot of thoughts. Proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the [criticism] and everything around, the way this team came together, and really turned the season around to get back into this position is something that was special, and we're not going to forget that. Obviously, it's not about doing amazing things in the regular season. It’s about the postseason.”

item.content:encoded:
Thin MLB crowds in Atlanta, Houston show challenge of selling afternoon Wild Card Series tickets
A late home run secured a playoff win for Atlanta; stadium attendance remains low for scheduled weekday afternoon games
- 1 minuto de lectura'
Austin Riley delivered the first clutch moment of Major League Baseball's playoffs on Tuesday, hitting a go-ahead three-run homer in the eighth inning that pushed the Atlanta Braves over the Philadelphia Phillies for a 5-3 win .
It was an electric scene for fans at Truist Park — at least for those who decided to show up.
There has been a noticeable number of empty seats in Atlanta and Houston for day games during this week's Wild Card Series, with the Braves drawing 30,127 fans for Game 1 on Tuesday that started at 2 p.m. local time, well below the 41,108 capacity. The Astros announced that 34,011 fans attended Tuesday's 4 p.m. Game 1 at Daikin Park, also well below its 41,168-seat limit.
It's not the first time this has happened.
Since MLB permanently expanded the playoffs to a 12-team bracket in 2022, just six of 26 afternoon Wild Card Series games through Tuesday have reached or exceeded stadium capacity. Seven games failed to reach even 85% capacity. The Braves-Phillies game on Tuesday was 73.2% full, which is the lowest since the postseason expanded, according to research from Sportradar.
Game 2 of the Braves-Phillies series had an announced crowd of 37,150 on Wednesday.
The main issue for day games is obvious: It's hard for fans to attend day games during the week — particularly in late September and October — because people have to work and children are back in school. It doesn't help that those game times are announced with only a few days' notice.
Still, it's a less-than-ideal atmosphere for some of the most important contests of the year.
Phillies third baseman Alec Bohm shrugged off the smaller crowds before Wednesday's game, saying his team just wants to win games and advance.
“I don’t think anybody on our team is really focused on how many people are showing up here," Bohm said. "It’s just kind of -- I think, like you said, it’s a 2 o’clock game in the middle of the week, so I think that might have something to do with it.
“That doesn’t take away from what’s going on on the field and kind of the stakes of all that in our minds.”
All three ALWCS games in Cleveland last year between the Guardians and Detroit Tigers started at 1:08 p.m., and none drew more than 30,000 fans. The Tampa Bay Rays had just 19,704 for an ALWCS opener against Texas in 2023 that started at 3:08 p.m., the lowest attendance for a non-COVID MLB postseason game since the 1919 World Series.
MLB declined to comment on the attendance numbers, but the league spreads its wild-card games throughout the day on purpose so they have their own television window and capture the largest viewing audience possible. NBC is paying the league roughly $200 million per year to host “Sunday Night Baseball” and the Wild Card Series during a three-year deal agreed to last November.
The Astros fans who did attend Tuesday's game were in a bit of a foul mood, peppering the team with boos as they fell behind 5-0 by the fifth inning on the way to a 6-3 loss. Astros manager Joe Espada said he understood the fans' frustration but hoped for a better atmosphere on Wednesday.
“I do want our fans to know that we love them and we need them,” Espada said. “They’re part of what we are trying to accomplish here. They’re part of our family.”
AP Sports Writers Charles Odum in Atlanta and Kristie Rieken in Houston contributed to this story.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz knows exactly what is at stake over the final days of the regular season.
After an injury-plagued year and an uneven return to the majors, the veteran reliever is trying to convince the Dodgers that he belongs in their postseason bullpen. Saturday brought another encouraging step in that direction.
Díaz worked a scoreless inning against the Giants and, more importantly, came away feeling that the fastball command that had eluded him earlier in the season is finally back.
“Yeah, 100%,” Díaz said when asked if he feels better now than he did before his latest stint in Triple-A. “I’ve been able to throw strikes. I think that was my problem, my concern. I wasn’t throwing my fastball for strikes. Now I’m able to command my fastball really good. And when I command my fastball, my slider plays up.”
That relationship between the two pitches is critical for Díaz. When the fastball is located properly, hitters have a much tougher time distinguishing it from his slider before the breaking ball dives away.
“Right now it’s really good,” Díaz said of the slider. “It’s going down and away. I’ve been able to throw my fastball glove side, so if I throw my fastball glove side, the slider will play off the same path.”
Díaz believes the improvement traces back to a mechanical adjustment made during his time at Oklahoma City.
Following a rough Triple-A appearance, he sat down with the pitching coaches and identified an issue with his hip movement and posture. He said the correction also helped restore an arm slot that had drifted earlier in the season.
“We found I wasn’t moving my hips the right way,” Díaz said. “We started working on that. On Tuesday I threw a really good pen. On Wednesday I pitched, I felt great, and lately I’ve been really good.”
The Dodgers have also been able to ease Díaz back into major league competition without immediately asking him to protect one-run leads in the ninth inning. He said he is perfectly comfortable with that arrangement.
“I’m open-minded right here,” Díaz said. “I need to help this team win. Whatever Doc puts me in the game, in any situation, I will do my job. I feel good. I just want to keep climbing the ladder and finish the season strong.”
That ladder could eventually lead to an October roster spot, but Díaz knows nothing has been guaranteed.
Dave Roberts has acknowledged that there is competition for the final places in a crowded Dodgers bullpen, and Díaz understands that his performance over these final games matters.
“I got to show them that I’m part of that bullpen,” Díaz said. “I haven’t pitched this year, and when I’ve been in the majors, I’ve been struggling. So right now I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot.”
For Díaz, the path from here is simple: keep throwing strikes, keep getting clean innings, and give the Dodgers a reason to trust him in October.
“Every time they give me the ball, in any situation, I will do my job,” he said. “And then at the end of the season, they will make decisions.”

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong's historic season just produced another staggering number, this time away from the baseball field.
The Chicago Cubs star's one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.098 million at Goldin.
The PSA Gem Mint 10 card, which also received a PSA 10 autograph grade, features the MLB Debut patch from Crow-Armstrong's first major-league game on September 11, 2023.
It is a massive sale by itself.
The timing makes it even more striking.
Crow-Armstrong just completed a historic 40-home run, 40-stolen base season and helped Chicago reach the postseason. Now, only days later, his signature rookie card has approached the MLB Debut Patch record while Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs enter an elimination game against the San Diego Padres.
$1,098,000: Winning bid for Pete Crow-Armstrong’s debut patch jersey tonight at @GoldinCo.
PCA’s 2024 rookie salary: $740,000. pic.twitter.com/d21WopsNpx
— Darren Rovell (@darrenrovell) September 30, 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong Card Sells for $1.098 Million
Crow-Armstrong's card was one of the most significant MLB Debut Patch cards to reach the market since Paul Skenes' one-of-one sold in 2025.
Goldin listed the card as Crow-Armstrong's 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph 1/1, graded PSA Gem Mint 10 with a PSA/DNA Gem Mint 10 autograph grade.
The $1.098 million result also produced a remarkable comparison highlighted by Rovell.
Crow-Armstrong earned roughly $740,000 during the 2024 season, meaning a collector just paid considerably more for his one-of-one rookie card than the Cubs paid Crow-Armstrong to play an entire major-league season.
But the final auction price may be even more notable for what it narrowly failed to accomplish.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Falls $12,000 Short of Paul Skenes Record
Crow-Armstrong came extraordinarily close to taking down the benchmark for MLB Debut Patch cards.
Skenes' one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.11 million through Fanatics Collect in March 2025. The price included the buyer's premium and established the Skenes card as the highest-selling MLB Debut Patch at the time.
Crow-Armstrong finished at $1.098 million.
The difference?
Just $12,000.
That puts Crow-Armstrong and Skenes in remarkably similar territory despite playing dramatically different positions and arriving in the majors with different levels of prospect hype.
Skenes was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 MLB Draft and won National League Rookie of the Year in his first season. His Debut Patch became a national story even before it surfaced, with the Pittsburgh Pirates famously offering the young collector who pulled it a package that included 30 years of season tickets.
Crow-Armstrong's card reached seven figures after a different catalyst: one of the greatest individual seasons ever produced by a Cubs player.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Made Cubs History Before $1.1 Million Sale
The auction could hardly have closed at a better moment for Crow-Armstrong's hobby profile.
On September 24, Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base of the season, joining the exclusive 40-40 club after already reaching 45 home runs.
He became just the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in the same season. He also became the first Cubs player to accomplish the feat.
And he did it on the same night Chicago clinched an NL Wild Card berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins.
Crow-Armstrong entered the postseason hitting .280 with 45 home runs and 107 RBIs while appearing in all 159 Cubs games through the clinching victory.
That transformed the timing of the Goldin auction.
Collectors were not merely bidding on the Debut Patch of a promising young Cubs player.
They were bidding on the Debut Patch of a 24-year-old who had just completed the first 40-40 season in franchise history.
Now the attention shifts back to what Crow-Armstrong can do on the field.
Cubs Face Elimination Against Padres After 8-0 Loss
Chicago enters Game 2 of its Wild Card Series against San Diego needing a victory to keep its season alive.
The Padres routed the Cubs 8-0 in Game 1 on September 29.
San Diego starter Michael King took a no-hit bid into the seventh inning and ultimately allowed only one hit over seven scoreless frames while striking out eight. Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts each homered for the Padres.
The Cubs will send Kevin Gausman to the mound for Game 2 opposite Nick Pivetta
There is at least one reason for optimism surrounding Crow-Armstrong specifically.
Chicago dominated San Diego during the regular season, winning five of six games and outscoring the Padres 55-28.
Crow-Armstrong was one of the Cubs' biggest problems for San Diego.
He hit .364 with four home runs in the six regular-season meetings.
Chicago will need another performance like that now.
Crow-Armstrong has already produced one of the defining baseball-card sales of 2026 and one of the most statistically significant seasons in Cubs history.
Whether his week is remembered primarily for a $1.098 million card sale or for what happens in October now depends on what Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs do next.

item.content:encoded:
Kyle Tucker is a four-time All-Star and one of the best outfielders in baseball when healthy.
His production during the 2026 regular season was not on par with what he accomplished earlier in his career.
This year was Tucker's first with the Los Angeles Dodgers. They likely imagined him as another superstar in a lineup that includes Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, and Freddie Freeman.
Unfortunately for the Dodgers, Tucker's offensive game took a significant step back.
"Well, the Dodgers could still three-peat, but it hasn't been a very impressive first season in Los Angeles for Tucker," Bleacher Report's Tim Kelly wrote.
Tucker played in 154 games and hit just 17 home runs, looking completely lost in right field at times.
"After signing a four-year, $240 million contract that includes a player opt-out after the second season, Tucker has produced just a 98 OPS+ in 2026," Kelly added. "Mind you, 100 is considered a league-average player, and Tucker averaged a 142 OPS+ from 2020-2025."
How can Tucker win back the trust of Dodgers fans?
MORE: Pirates urged to re-sign Brandon Lowe if they ‘want to be taken seriously’
A strong postseason would be an excellent starting point.
"Tucker is finishing the season on a high note, as he has a .921 OPS in September. If he has a big October, no one will remember how much he struggled during the regular season," Kelly wrote. "But this has definitely been an underwhelming campaign for the four-time All-Star."
The Dodgers are a threat to win a third consecutive championship. If Tucker can carry his success from September to October, Los Angeles will be very hard to dethrone.

NEW YORK – One year later, they’re right back at it. The Yankees are preparing to host the Red Sox for another American League Wild Card Series, renewing baseball’s most enduring rivalry in a best-of-three showdown.
Tuesday’s Game 1 delivers a rematch of the pairing that took place in the Bronx last October, when Cam Schlittler struck out 12 over eight scoreless innings to quiet the online chirpers and end Boston’s season, propelling his Yankees into the AL Division Series.
This time, the prize is a trip to Tropicana Field, where the Rays will be waiting to face the winner. These Yankees would gladly sign up for that.
“It's special,” Schlittler said on Monday. “Being able to get that experience last year in Game 3, it's a good feeling to go out there and get the first one.”
You don’t need to flip back to Bucky Dent to find the latest great comeback. These Red Sox seemed to have one foot on the golf course in late June, a managerial change already having taken place as they faced a 15 1/2-game deficit in the division on June 19. They rescued their season, beginning with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park from June 25-28.
“I’ve been watching Red Sox-Yankees since I was a kid. It’s Red Sox-Yankees,” said Tracy. “It’s no secret as far as the rivalry that has existed over the years for a very long time. That’s obvious to everybody. I know there’s always a little extra when those two teams meet. Beyond that, I’m not putting much more into that other than just preparing and getting ready for that series.”
How can I tune in?
Game 1 of the Red Sox-Yankees Wild Card Series is underway at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Tolle has become a fireballing fan favorite in Boston, just as likely to strike someone out on a 98 mph heater as he is to wrap someone into a bear hug. The Red Sox have no reservations about putting the 23-year-old into the hostile territory Yankee Stadium figures to be.
Gray, at 36, is having one of the best seasons of his career in his first year with Boston. He easily leads the Red Sox in quality starts with 20. The Yankees are one of his former teams, and the only one he didn’t perform well for in his career.
Starting pitching is the Yanks’ greatest strength going into this postseason. Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) built upon his 2025 playoff breakout to establish his place among the league’s most dominant young arms. The Walpole, Mass., product relishes taking on the Sox, for whom he once cheered, and will likely use whatever vitriol he can find on social media as potential rage fuel.
Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA) will follow in Game 2, with Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA) in line for Game 3. Fried has faced Boston twice this year, including eight scoreless innings on April 22 at Fenway Park. He last pitched Sept. 22 vs. the Rays, allowing four runs in 6 2/3 innings. Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA) is likely to be available out of the bullpen as he prepares for a potential ALDS Game 1.
What are the starting lineups?
Red Sox: Schlittler has been a big-time nemesis for the Red Sox, dating back to his coming-out party in the playoffs last year. But Boston did get a jolt from Caleb Durbin in the form of a go-ahead homer over the Green Monster against the Yankees’ ace on June 25, the win that started the 32-5 run by the Red Sox. Recently, Boston hitters have worked overtime on the Trajekt pitching machine, which can mimic any Major League starting pitcher. The Sox have struggled offensively for much of September, particularly with runners in scoring position. But they’ve also lacked multiple key lineup pieces at various parts of the month.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone said the Yankees view Tolle as “closer to neutral” in terms of splits, but they also tried to load their lineup with right-handed bats when they faced him in June. They did that again in Game 1, with Anthony Volpe getting the start over Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second base and Amed Rosario inserted at third base.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Red Sox: Aroldis Chapman, a former Yankee, continues to be one of the elite closers in the game at 38 years old. He has one of the league’s best setup men in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. In a significant development, the Sox placed their other key high-leverage reliever -- righty Tyron Guerrero, who frequents triple digits with his fastball -- back on the 15-day IL with a right shoulder and lat strain on Sunday’s final day of the regular season. Brayan Bello is the Swiss Army knife of the bullpen, available for bulk relief and also taking down a couple of innings when necessary. The most intriguing roster question for the Red Sox heading into the series was answered Tuesday morning, when Garrett Crochet, who started the season as the ace but hasn’t pitched since April 25, was activated for this series.
Yankees: David Bednar finished his first full season in the Bronx with 35 saves and a 2.50 ERA in 63 appearances, the closer ahead of a relief crew that leaned heavily upon Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick and Tim Hill in the late innings. The Yankees didn’t make a bullpen acquisition at the Trade Deadline, but they added pieces down the stretch by picking up Michael Fulmer and John Schreiber, both of whom could be called upon for valuable outs. Will Warren is also converting into a relief role and could provide length. Ryan Weathers appears to be in play as a potential bullpen piece, adding a big arm to the mix.
Any injuries of note?
Red Sox: Contreras got smoked on the knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie on Sept. 17, but took two at-bats in the final game of the regular season on Sunday and should be good to go. Guerrero is a big loss in the bullpen for this series. Justin Slaten, a key leverage reliever for Boston the past three seasons, is also out with a right flexor injury.
Masataka Yoshida, one of the few Boston hitters who performed against the Yankees in last year’s postseason series, won’t factor in this year. He’s been out since Aug. 16 with a hamstring strain and likely won’t make it back this season.
Yankees: No story has occupied more space recently than Aaron Judge’s right soleus strain, which typically requires weeks on the injured list. Judge tried to convince the Yankees' brass that he could give it a go for the Wild Card round, but sources confirmed to MLB.com on Tuesday that Judge would would not be on the Wild Card roster vs. Boston. Meanwhile, Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham have both been hitting and running. Weathers is out with a flexor strain but hopes to return.
Who is hot and who is not?
Red Sox: Anthony has understandably had some ups and downs after missing nearly four months with a right hand/wrist injury, but he slashed .333/.375/.633 in his final eight games of the season. From a pitching standpoint, Bello has been a force since he returned from the Minors, posting a 2.11 ERA in 14 appearances, including three starts.
Rutschman has had a hard time getting his bat going since joining the Red Sox at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline but had a two-hit game in Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader against the Cubs. Abreu is notoriously streaky and he’s been mostly cold in September (.207/.286/.329, one homer, six RBIs). If past history is any indication, he could heat up again in a hurry.
Yankees: Rice hit his team-leading 40th and 41st home runs on Sept. 23 vs. Tampa Bay, claiming a share of the AL lead until Pete Alonso passed him on Friday. Rice, a Cohasset, Mass., product, has belted six homers in September. Bellinger has been productive all month, tying Jones (14) for second on the team in RBIs behind Lombard (16). García enjoyed a productive stretch after arriving in a midseason trade but recently endured a long hitless streak. Ryan McMahon has struggled to produce all year.
Anything else fans might want to know?
This marks the seventh time the rivalry has gone to the postseason stage – all since 1999. Fittingly, the teams have split the first six matchups.
The Yankees had the series edge over Boston this season, winning seven of 13 contests. The Yanks swept three games at Fenway in April and split a pair in June, then were swept in a four-game series in Boston later that month. New York took three of four from the Sox in late August, their most recent meeting.
Though Anthony was a big part of the ‘25 Red Sox team, he missed the postseason with a left oblique strain. He is Boston’s leadoff hitter and could have a big impact on this series. During the World Baseball Classic for Team USA, Anthony displayed the ability to perform on a big stage.

Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

The MLB playoffs begin today!! (September, 29.) The action begins with the National League Wild Card matchup between the Atlanta Braves and the Philadelphia Phillies.
First pitch is at 2:15 p.m. EST, and both teams are deploying very formidable starters. For Atlanta, it is rolling with Chris Sale in the series opener, and the Phillies are opting to go with Jesus Luzardo as their starter.
Both teams have officially announced their lineup, and for the Braves, the lineup drop features a notable Austin Riley decision.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Suddenly Add 6-Year MLB Veteran Before Phillies WC Series
Braves' Austin Riley Batting 7th in Series Opener
In the NLWC series opener against the Phillies, Austin Riley will bat seventh and play third base, which isn't a huge surprise.
Here is the full Atlanta Braves batting order, per @UnderdogMLB:
"Braves 9/29 D. Baldwin C R. Acuña Jr. RF M. Olson 1B M. Dubón LF M. Harris II CF O. Albies 2B A. Riley 3B M. Yastrzemski DH H. Kim SS C. Sale SP"
A few lineup notes: Mike Yastrzemski gets the start at DH, with the anticipation that Luzardo won't throw very long, and Ha-Seong Kim gets the start at SS. Mauricio Dubon is the team's cleanup hitter, and Ozzie Albies (who crushes lefties) will bat sixth.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Quietly Cut Ties with 27-Year-Old Player Before Phillies Playoff Series
Looking at Austin Riley's 2026 Season
Now that the regular season is officially in the books, we can take a look at Austin Riley's season as a whole.
Over 159 games played and 566 total at-bats, Austin Riley batted .219 with 19 home runs and a career-low OPS+ of 80.
He also added 21 doubles, 72 RBI, 64 runs scored, and 124 hits to the Braves' regular-season offense.
However, the regular season is in the past, and Austin Riley can write all those wrongs by having a big moment or two in the MLB playoffs. Riley would likely be the first to admit he had a poor offensive season, but October baseball can bring a breath of fresh air to players who struggled over the past several months.

The Houston Astros enter the postseason with the AL MVP favorite in their lineup.
Yordan Alvarez should be considered the most feared hitter in baseball for this year's playoffs.
But the rest of Houston's lineup has been mediocre at best.
"The Astros have the presumptive AL MVP in Yordan Alvarez, but the rest of the offense has produced a .233/.300/.396 line this year," Bleacher Report's Joel Reuter wrote. "He will need to replicate his memorable performance in the 2023 ALCS for pretty much the entirety of October."
Clearly, the Astros rely on Alvarez to do most of their offensive damage, but he may not be the AL West club's "X-Factor" during the Wild Card Series against the Chicago White Sox.
Instead, Reuter has tabbed rookie center fielder Lucas Spence as someone who can help Houston make a deep postseason run.
"Lucas Spence went 6-for-18 with four home runs in five games after being recalled from Triple-A when [Daulton] Varsho and [Brice] Matthews were placed on the injured list," Reuter added. "He suddenly looks like the no-doubt starting center fielder for the club's playoff run."
MORE: Pirates urged to re-sign Brandon Lowe if they ‘want to be taken seriously’
Varsho is unavailable in the Wild Card Series due to left wrist inflammation caused by cysts.
He is a Gold Glove outfielder but has hit poorly following a midseason trade from the Toronto Blue Jays.
Spence has just 19 MLB games under his belt but looks up for the challenge, hitting the first three home runs of his career in a single game during the last week of the regular season against the Athletics.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — The playoffs have arrived.
The Cubs have been building to this all season long, eyeing a run deep into October.
‘‘This group is ready,’’ catcher Carson Kelly said Sunday. ‘‘It’s been a long year. We’ve had our ups and downs. But what this group does really well is we come prepared every single day.’’
To get to where they want to go, the Cubs first need to get past the Padres, their opponent in a best-of-three wild-card series.
Here’s what could make the difference:
Pete Crow-Armstrong
Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball this season and soon will have an MVP award on his mantel to show for it.
But the individual accolades have meant little to Crow-Armstrong, given that he’s focused on team goals. The chase for the biggest of those — a World Series title — starts now.
It’s a team sport, and everyone will have to do their job for the Cubs to win. But if you’re going to talk about the impact one player can make, Crow-Armstrong can make more than just about anyone else in the playoffs.
‘‘We’re fortunate we get to see it in person every single day,’’ Kelly said. ‘‘There are a lot of times where we’ll look at each other and say, ‘Oh, my gosh, did that really just happen?’
‘‘Sometimes he gets up there, and you’re like, ‘OK, Pete’s going to hit a homer.’ He hits it, and you’re like, ‘What?’ Or running a ball down in the gap. Stealing a base, stealing second and third. You’re like, ‘This guy, he does it all.’ ’’
Alex Bregman
A week ago, the Cubs didn’t know what Bregman would be able to give them, if anything, in the postseason after taking a foul ball off his face.
But not only are they able to include Bregman in their playoff plans, they can count him as a
centerpiece.
A week removed from his freak injury, Bregman homered twice as part of a four-hit Sunday.
San Diego. Drink it in. It always goes down smooth. Just like these couple two tree things about the Cubs the night before the playoffs start. @suntimes_sports @Suntimes pic.twitter.com/2j45VXUP43
— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) September 29, 2026
Bregman got back to being Bregman in a hurry, and that’s a big deal. The Cubs signed him to a five-year, $175 million free-agent deal in part to be a force in October, where he’s one of the most accomplished postseason hitters of all time.
And showing some Chicago toughness helps, too.
‘‘It fires you up,’’ Crow-Armstrong said Monday. ‘‘Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is about his work and how much he loves the game, it’s not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is, him coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, I’m just not that surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.
‘‘Most important, I’m glad he’s healthy enough to do what he loves. But selfishly, I’m pumped that he’s going to be in our lineup for these important games. Simply put, Alex Bregman makes our lineup better, so it’s huge he’s getting himself game-ready.’’
The bullpen
It wasn’t long ago that the Cubs’ bullpen was in disarray.
But things have stabilized a bit, with manager Craig Counsell leaning on right-handers Ryan Zeferjahn (1.13 ERA in his last nine outings) and Daniel Palencia (eight scoreless appearances in a row) to great effect.
Palencia is looking more like the guy who dazzled last season, and Zeferjahn is looking more like the guy the Cubs thought they landed in a deadline deal.
‘‘He’s had some good outings lately,’’ Counsell said of Zeferjahn. ‘‘I feel great about him. He’s going to pitch. He’s going to be a major part of this at the end here.’’
The Cubs don’t necessarily have a designated closer, not that they see that as a problem, given Counsell’s ‘‘out-getters’’ mantra. But should any fans fret that is the team’s Achilles’ heel, maybe Zeferjahn can put their minds at ease.
‘‘There’s ups and downs, and I rode that ‘down’ for a little bit,’’ Zeferjahn said. ‘‘But I’ve been working my way back up. . . . Hopefully, I’m riding an all-time high here going into the playoffs.’’
The conditions
The Cubs led baseball in runs scored this season, but the bats didn’t look great last week, averaging just two runs a game.
But heading to San Diego could have its advantages.
Kelly compared trying to hit at Wrigley Field and Fenway Park last week — they scored nine total runs in five games at the cold, windy venues — “like you’re hitting into a fan.”
The Cubs moved indoors Sunday and scored six runs. That’s only one game, hardly an indicator of what’s to come. But not dealing with poor hitting conditions is one way to allow a capable Cubs lineup to flex its muscles.
The catch? They might have to get real muscly, as the Padres — quite used to hitting in nice weather — have been on a roll, with only one team in baseball (the Brewers) scoring more runs in September.

Cal Raleigh was still processing the news of Dan Wilson’s departure when he was asked Sunday afternoon if he wanted to be involved in the search for the next Seattle Mariners manager.
“It’s uncharted territory for me,” the Mariners catcher said. “So I don’t really necessarily know how that goes at this level. We’ll just have to see how it plays out. I’m sure they’ll probably start looking right away.”
The search for Wilson’s successor is expected to begin in earnest this week.
Neither of the Mariners’ last two managers — Scott Servais and Dan Wilson — had experience managing in the big leagues before taking over the Mariners’ job. It would seem likely that that would be a priority for the club this time around.
That in mind, here’s a list of candidates likely to pique the Mariners’ interest:
Torey Lovullo
The Mariners front office has already had internal discussions about Lovullo, the Diamondbacks manager who appears to be a leading candidate for the job, according to industry sources.
Lovullo’s status in Arizona, as of Sunday, was uncertain. His contract expires at the end of this season, and there have reportedly been no talks about a new contract for him there. The Diamondbacks were eliminated from playoff contention on Sunday after finishing 86-76.
The D’backs have missed the playoffs in each of the past three seasons after Lovullo led them to the 2023 National League pennant.
Lovullo has a 750-768 record in 10 seasons as the D’backs manager.
“I want to win a world championship with this organization,” Lovullo told reportedly Sunday. “But I want to be wanted. I’ll just leave it at that. (My job) is probably not the conversation to have right now. I need to think about a few things.”
Stephen Vogt
To be clear: This appears highly unlikely. Vogt, the Guardians manager, would almost certainly be No. 1 on the Mariners’ wish list — No. 1 on any team’s list, probably — if he were available. But that’s a big if.
Vogt, the AL Manager of the Year in 2024 and ’25, has led the Guardians to the AL Central title in all three years as manager, and he reportedly signed a multiyear extension before the 2025 season. Vogt has strong ties to the Puget Sound area; his wife is from Olympia and the family lives in Olympia during the offseason. Vogt was the Mariners’ bullpen coach in ’23 and was in line to take over as Seattle’s bench coach alongside Scott Servais in ’24 before the Guardians hired him as manager.
Presuming Vogt is still under contract with Cleveland for 2027, it would require some sort of trade. Manager trades are rare, though not unprecedented. The Mariners famously traded Lou Piniella to Tampa Bay for All-Star left fielder Randy Winn in October 2002. (Two other managers have been traded since — Ozzie Guillen from the White Sox to the Marlins in 2011, and John Farrell from the Blue Jays to the Red Sox in 2012.) But, again, it does seem highly unlikely in this case; what would be the Guardians’ motivation be to move on from one of the sport’s best managers?
Kristopher Negrón
A Pirates bench coach, Negrón, 40, has deep ties with the Mariners.
He was hired as the Mariners’ assistant director of player development in 2019, the Triple-A Tacoma manager in 2021 and a member of the Mariners major-league coaching staff from 2022-25, serving as the first base and third base coach. (He was acting manager for a brief period in 2022 when Servais and Manny Acta contracted COVID-19.)
The Pirates hired Negrón last offseason to be their bench coach, and he’s long been viewed as a coach on the rise in the industry.
Rocco Baldelli
A baseball operations assistant with the Dodgers, Baldelli, 45, compiled a 527-505 record (. 511) in seven seasons as Minnesota’s manager. In his first year, he was named AL Manager of the Year in 2019 after leading the Twins to 101 wins.
Tampa’s first-round pick in 2000, Baldelli played seven years in the majors as an outfielder, then in retirement spent seven more seasons with Rays as a minor-league coordinator and major-league coach.
He’s now in his first season as a special assistant in the Dodgers’ front office.
Kai Correa
A Mets bench coach, Correa, 38, played college baseball at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma from 2007-2010, then began his coaching career there.
He got his first job in MLB as a minor-league coach in Cleveland’s organization in 2018.
At age 31, he became baseball’s youngest bench coach when he joined San Francisco in that role in 2020. He spent four seasons with the Giants before returning to Cleveland to be their major-league field coordinator in 2024-25.
He just completed his first season as the Mets bench coach.
Other names to watch
• Chris Woodward, Dodgers first base coach; former Rangers manager; former Mariners first base coach.
• Brandon Hyde, Rays senior adviser; former Orioles manager
• Andy McKay, Guardians field coordinator; former Mariners assistant GM
